ora-1: 1) This error's own `params` and `info` fields carry Oracle's queries for identifying the constraint, its table and its columns -- start there. 2) Find the duplicates already present: `SELECT <cols>, COUNT(*) FROM <owner>.<table> GROUP BY <cols> HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;` 3) Confirm whether it is a constraint or a unique index: `SELECT 'CONSTRAINT' FROM dba_constraints WHERE owner = UPPER('<o>') AND constraint_name = UPPER('<n>') UNION ALL SELECT 'INDEX' FROM dba_indexes WHERE owner = UPPER('<o>') AND index_name = UPPER('<n>');` 4) For bulk loads, isolate the bad rows instead of failing the statement: `INSERT /*+ APPEND */ INTO <t> SELECT ... LOG ERRORS INTO <err_table> ('<tag>') REJECT LIMIT UNLIMITED;` (create the error table first with `EXEC DBMS_ERRLOG.CREATE_ERROR_LOG('<t>');`) 5) Where an upsert is intended, use MERGE rather than INSERT plus exception handling. 6) On 23ai the violating values are printed in the message when ERROR_MESSAGE_DETAILS is ON (the default): `ALTER SESSION SET ERROR_MESSAGE_DETAILS = ON;` 7) If a sequence-backed surrogate key is colliding, check that the sequence was not reset below MAX(id) after an import.
ora-18: 1) Check the ceiling and the peak: `SELECT resource_name, current_utilization, max_utilization, limit_value FROM v$resource_limit WHERE resource_name IN ('sessions','processes');` 2) Find where the sessions come from: `SELECT username, program, machine, status, COUNT(*) FROM v$session GROUP BY username, program, machine, status ORDER BY 5 DESC;` 3) Long-idle INACTIVE sessions point at a connection pool that never releases: `SELECT sid, username, machine, status, last_call_et/3600 idle_hours FROM v$session WHERE status = 'INACTIVE' AND last_call_et > 3600 ORDER BY last_call_et DESC;` 4) Raise the limit -- sessions derives from processes, so set processes: `ALTER SYSTEM SET processes = <n> SCOPE=SPFILE;` then restart the instance. 5) Size the pool to the workload rather than raising the limit repeatedly; every process costs PGA, so an oversized pool trades this error for ORA-04030.
ora-20: 1) Identical handling to ORA-00018. `SELECT resource_name, current_utilization, max_utilization, limit_value FROM v$resource_limit WHERE resource_name IN ('processes','sessions');` 2) Note that background and parallel query processes count against this limit: `SELECT program, COUNT(*) FROM v$process GROUP BY program ORDER BY 2 DESC;` A parallel-heavy workload can exhaust processes without any growth in user connections. 3) Connect as SYSDBA through the preallocated slot if you are locked out: `sqlplus / as sysdba` on the host. 4) `ALTER SYSTEM SET processes = <n> SCOPE=SPFILE;` then restart. 5) Check parallel_max_servers against processes -- the two must be sized together.
ora-52: 1) Check the limit: `SELECT resource_name, current_utilization, max_utilization, limit_value FROM v$resource_limit WHERE resource_name LIKE 'enqueue%';` 2) On modern releases enqueue resources are derived from processes, sessions and transactions rather than set directly -- raising processes is normally the fix: `ALTER SYSTEM SET processes = <n> SCOPE=SPFILE;` 3) Look for a session holding an unusual number of locks: `SELECT sid, COUNT(*) FROM v$lock GROUP BY sid ORDER BY 2 DESC FETCH FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY;` 4) A runaway job taking per-row locks or a very large transaction is the usual cause; fix that rather than the parameter.
ora-54: 1) Find the blocker directly: `SELECT sid, serial#, username, blocking_session, blocking_instance, event, sql_id FROM v$session WHERE blocking_session IS NOT NULL;` 2) Identify the locked object: `SELECT s.sid, s.username, s.program, o.owner, o.object_name, l.type, l.lmode, l.request FROM v$lock l JOIN v$session s ON s.sid = l.sid JOIN dba_objects o ON o.object_id = l.id1 WHERE l.type IN ('TM','TX');` 3) Wait, or terminate the holder: `ALTER SYSTEM KILL SESSION '<sid>,<serial#>' IMMEDIATE;` 4) The better fix for DDL is to queue rather than fail: `ALTER SESSION SET ddl_lock_timeout = 60;` 5) Prefer online DDL where the edition supports it -- `ALTER TABLE ... MOVE ONLINE`, `ALTER INDEX ... REBUILD ONLINE`, `ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... ENABLE NOVALIDATE` -- and schedule the rest in a quiet window. 6) An unindexed foreign key makes a child-table DML take a full table lock on the parent, which shows up here; check for missing FK indexes.
ora-60: 1) Oracle has already broken the deadlock by rolling back one statement -- the application must retry. The task now is to stop it recurring. 2) Read the trace file named in the alert log; it contains the deadlock graph with both sessions, their rows and their SQL: `SELECT value FROM v$diag_info WHERE name = 'Diag Trace';` 3) A 'TX ... mode 4' deadlock in the graph points at an unindexed foreign key. Find them: `SELECT c.owner, c.table_name, c.constraint_name FROM dba_constraints c WHERE c.constraint_type = 'R' AND c.owner = UPPER('<o>');` then confirm each child FK column list has a leading-edge index in dba_ind_columns. 4) A 'TX ... mode 6' deadlock is usually the application updating the same rows in different orders in two transactions -- impose a consistent ordering (for example, always update by ascending primary key). 5) Shorten transactions and avoid user think-time between the first DML and the COMMIT. 6) Check for bitmap indexes on a table taking concurrent DML -- they lock whole key ranges and deadlock readily.
ora-257: 1) The database has stopped accepting DML. Check the recovery area first: `SELECT name, space_limit/1024/1024/1024 limit_gb, space_used/1024/1024/1024 used_gb, ROUND(space_used/space_limit*100, 1) pct FROM v$recovery_file_dest;` 2) Check every archive destination for an error: `SELECT dest_id, dest_name, status, error FROM v$archive_dest WHERE status <> 'INACTIVE';` 3) See what is consuming the FRA: `SELECT file_type, percent_space_used, percent_space_reclaimable, number_of_files FROM v$flash_recovery_area_usage;` 4) The correct fix is to back up and remove archivelogs, not to delete files at the OS level: `RMAN> BACKUP ARCHIVELOG ALL DELETE INPUT;` or `RMAN> DELETE ARCHIVELOG ALL COMPLETED BEFORE 'SYSDATE-1';` 5) For immediate relief while a backup runs: `ALTER SYSTEM SET db_recovery_file_dest_size = <n>G SCOPE=BOTH;` 6) On a Data Guard primary, archivelogs are not reclaimable until the standby has applied them -- `SELECT thread#, MAX(sequence#) FROM v$archived_log WHERE applied = 'YES' GROUP BY thread#;` A stalled standby is a common cause of a full FRA. 7) If files were removed outside RMAN, the catalog still counts them: `RMAN> CROSSCHECK ARCHIVELOG ALL; DELETE EXPIRED ARCHIVELOG ALL;`
ora-600: 1) An internal consistency check failed. The first argument identifies the specific defect and is the only part that makes this diagnosable -- capture the full argument list from the alert log. 2) Locate the trace and incident: `SELECT name, value FROM v$diag_info WHERE name IN ('Diag Trace','Diag Alert','ADR Home');` then `adrci> show incident` 3) Look the first argument up in My Oracle Support Doc 153788.1 (ORA-600/ORA-7445 Lookup Tool) -- many are known bugs with a patch or a workaround. 4) Package diagnostics for support: `adrci> ips pack incident <n> in /tmp` 5) Do not restart reflexively. If it is reproducible, capture the incident first; a restart can clear the evidence without clearing the cause. 6) Judge the blast radius: ORA-00600 during redo apply or on a SYSTEM datafile is an availability event; one raised by a single session on one query usually is not. Check whether the instance stayed up: `SELECT instance_name, status, startup_time FROM v$instance;` 7) Check for related corruption: `SELECT * FROM v$database_block_corruption;` 8) Open an SR with the packaged incident; ORA-00600 is a defect by definition.
ora-752: 1) Serious: the storage acknowledged a write that it did not persist. Do not simply restart and continue. 2) The alert log names the file and block. Cross-check: `SELECT * FROM v$database_block_corruption;` 3) On a standby detecting this during redo apply, the primary is the one with the lost write. Failing over to the standby is frequently safer than repairing the primary in place. 4) Restore and recover the affected datafile from backup: `RMAN> RESTORE DATAFILE <f>; RECOVER DATAFILE <f>;` 5) Validate the rest of the database before returning it to service: `RMAN> BACKUP VALIDATE CHECK LOGICAL DATABASE;` 6) Investigate the storage and firmware path -- lost writes come from the array, HBA, or a volume manager, not from Oracle. 7) Confirm protection is enabled going forward: `SHOW PARAMETER db_lost_write_protect` (set to TYPICAL or FULL) along with db_block_checksum. 8) Open a support SR; lost-write incidents warrant vendor analysis of the storage stack.
ora-942: 1) Confirm the object exists and who owns it: `SELECT owner, object_name, object_type, status FROM dba_objects WHERE object_name = UPPER('<name>');` 2) If it exists but under another schema, the caller needs a privilege and usually a synonym: `GRANT SELECT ON <owner>.<obj> TO <user>;` then `CREATE SYNONYM <user>.<obj> FOR <owner>.<obj>;` (or a public synonym). 3) Check what the caller can actually see: `SELECT * FROM all_objects WHERE object_name = UPPER('<name>');` run as that user -- this is the definitive test. 4) Inside definer-rights PL/SQL, privileges held through a role do not apply. Grant directly to the owner of the procedure, or make it AUTHID CURRENT_USER if that matches the design. 5) A quoted, mixed-case identifier must be quoted everywhere: an object created as "MyTable" is not reachable as MyTable. 6) ORA-00942 is also raised for a DML privilege the user lacks even when SELECT is granted -- check `SELECT privilege FROM dba_tab_privs WHERE table_name = UPPER('<name>') AND grantee = UPPER('<user>');`
ora-955: 1) Find the conflict: `SELECT owner, object_name, object_type, created FROM dba_objects WHERE object_name = UPPER('<name>');` 2) Remember that tables, views, sequences, synonyms and private synonyms all share one namespace per schema. 3) Check the recyclebin -- a dropped object still holds its name until purged: `SELECT object_name, original_name, type, droptime FROM dba_recyclebin WHERE original_name = UPPER('<name>');` then `PURGE TABLE <name>;` or `PURGE RECYCLEBIN;` 4) A public synonym can collide with a local object name: `SELECT * FROM dba_synonyms WHERE synonym_name = UPPER('<name>');` 5) In a repeatable deployment script, guard the create or drop first rather than relying on the error.
ora-1000: 1) Check the limit and the peak: `SELECT value FROM v$parameter WHERE name = 'open_cursors';` and `SELECT resource_name, current_utilization, max_utilization, limit_value FROM v$resource_limit WHERE resource_name = 'open_cursors';` 2) Find the offending sessions: `SELECT s.sid, s.username, s.program, COUNT(*) cursors FROM v$open_cursor c JOIN v$session s ON s.sid = c.sid GROUP BY s.sid, s.username, s.program ORDER BY cursors DESC;` 3) Find the repeated statement -- a leak usually shows one SQL held hundreds of times: `SELECT sql_text, COUNT(*) FROM v$open_cursor WHERE sid = <sid> GROUP BY sql_text ORDER BY 2 DESC;` 4) Raising the parameter buys time but does not fix a leak: `ALTER SYSTEM SET open_cursors = <n> SCOPE=BOTH;` 5) The real fix is in the application -- close ResultSets and Statements in a finally block, and do not create a new PreparedStatement inside a loop. In PL/SQL, close explicit cursors and avoid ref cursors that escape scope. 6) Check session_cached_cursors too; an oversized cache inflates open cursor counts.
ora-1017: 1) Check the account before assuming a wrong password -- a locked or expired account can surface as ORA-01017 in some drivers: `SELECT username, account_status, lock_date, expiry_date, profile FROM dba_users WHERE username = UPPER('<user>');` 2) Passwords are case-sensitive (sec_case_sensitive_logon / SQLNET.ALLOWED_LOGON_VERSION_SERVER). A credential that worked before an upgrade and fails after it is usually a case or password-version mismatch: `SELECT username, password_versions FROM dba_users WHERE username = UPPER('<user>');` 3) Review recent failures to see where they come from: `SELECT dbusername, userhost, client_program_name, event_timestamp FROM unified_audit_trail WHERE return_code = 1017 ORDER BY event_timestamp DESC FETCH FIRST 20 ROWS ONLY;` (or dba_audit_session on older releases). 4) Confirm the client reached the intended database: `SELECT sys_context('USERENV','DB_NAME') db, sys_context('USERENV','SERVICE_NAME') svc FROM dual;` A correct password against the wrong environment looks identical to a bad password. 5) For SYSDBA connections, check the password file rather than dba_users: `SELECT * FROM v$pwfile_users;` 6) Repeated failures will lock the account once FAILED_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS is reached -- find and fix the stale credential (app server, cron job, monitoring agent) before it does.
ora-1031: 1) Find what the user actually has: `SELECT privilege FROM dba_sys_privs WHERE grantee = UPPER('<user>');` `SELECT granted_role FROM dba_role_privs WHERE grantee = UPPER('<user>');` `SELECT owner, table_name, privilege FROM dba_tab_privs WHERE grantee = UPPER('<user>');` 2) The most common cause is a privilege granted through a role: roles are disabled inside definer-rights PL/SQL and in some DDL contexts. Grant it directly to the user instead of through a role. 3) For SYSDBA or SYSOPER, the check is the password file or OS group, not dba_sys_privs: `SELECT * FROM v$pwfile_users;` and confirm the OS user is in the dba group. Also check `SHOW PARAMETER remote_login_passwordfile`. 4) A DDL failure on someone else's object needs an ANY-scoped privilege (ALTER ANY TABLE, CREATE ANY INDEX). 5) CREATE TABLE succeeding but the segment failing is a quota problem, not a privilege one -- see ORA-01950. 6) In a CDB, a common user needs the privilege granted with CONTAINER=ALL to use it in a PDB.
ora-1033: 1) The instance is not open for this connection. From a SYSDBA session on the host: `SELECT instance_name, status, database_status FROM v$instance;` and `SELECT name, open_mode FROM v$database;` 2) If it is stuck in MOUNT, the alert log says why -- usually recovery in progress or a datafile that cannot be opened: `SELECT file#, error, online_status FROM v$recover_file;` 3) Open it once mount completes: `ALTER DATABASE OPEN;` 4) During a normal startup or shutdown this is transient and correct -- clients should retry. 5) On a physical standby open read-only, write connections get this legitimately; route them to the primary. 6) In a CDB, check the PDB rather than the CDB: `SELECT name, open_mode, restricted FROM v$pdbs;` and `ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE <pdb> OPEN;`
ora-1110: 1) ORA-01110 is always a companion to a more specific error -- find that error in the stack or alert log and treat it as the real one (commonly ORA-01578, ORA-01113, ORA-27037, ORA-01157). 2) Identify the file and its state: `SELECT file#, name, status, enabled FROM v$datafile WHERE file# = <n>;` 3) Check whether it needs recovery: `SELECT file#, error, online_status, change# FROM v$recover_file;` 4) `SELECT tablespace_name, file_name, online_status FROM dba_data_files WHERE file_id = <n>;` 5) Verify the file is present and readable at the OS or ASM layer before any recovery action.
ora-1400: 1) The message names the column. Confirm the definition: `SELECT column_name, nullable, data_default FROM dba_tab_columns WHERE owner = UPPER('<o>') AND table_name = UPPER('<t>') AND nullable = 'N';` 2) Supply the value, or give the column a default: `ALTER TABLE <o>.<t> MODIFY (<col> DEFAULT <value>);` -- in 12c+ `DEFAULT ON NULL` also substitutes when an explicit NULL is supplied. 3) Relax the constraint only if the model allows: `ALTER TABLE <o>.<t> MODIFY (<col> NULL);` 4) In an ETL context a NULL here usually means a source column was renamed, a join dropped rows, or a mapping drifted -- check the source rather than the target. 5) For a trigger-populated column, confirm the trigger is enabled: `SELECT trigger_name, status FROM dba_triggers WHERE table_name = UPPER('<t>');`
ora-1438:
1) The message gives the value, the precision and the column. Check the definition: `SELECT column_name, data_type, data_precision, data_scale FROM dba_tab_columns WHERE owner = UPPER('') AND table_name = UPPER('');` 2) Note that NUMBER(p,s) limits the digits left of the decimal to p-s -- NUMBER(5,2) holds at most 999.99, not 99999.99. This is the usual surprise. 3) Find the offending source rows before widening anything: `SELECT * FROM WHERE ABS() >= POWER(10,

- );` 4) Widen if the value is legitimate: `ALTER TABLE . MODIFY ( NUMBER(

,));` -- widening is online and does not rewrite the table. 5) If the value is not legitimate, fix the calculation; a rounding or unit error (cents vs dollars) is common.
ora-1536: 1) This is a per-user quota, not a full tablespace. Check it: `SELECT username, tablespace_name, bytes/1024/1024 used_mb, max_bytes/1024/1024 max_mb FROM dba_ts_quotas WHERE username = UPPER('<user>');` -- max_bytes of -1 means UNLIMITED. 2) Compare against what the schema already holds: `SELECT SUM(bytes)/1024/1024 mb FROM dba_segments WHERE owner = UPPER('<user>') AND tablespace_name = '<ts>';` 3) Raise the quota: `ALTER USER <user> QUOTA <n>G ON <ts>;` or `ALTER USER <user> QUOTA UNLIMITED ON <ts>;` 4) If the quota is deliberate, reclaim inside the schema instead -- drop or truncate unused segments, or move the object to another tablespace. 5) Confirm the tablespace itself still has room; if it does not, the next failure will be ORA-01653.
ora-1552: 1) The instance is using the SYSTEM rollback segment because no undo tablespace is online. `SELECT tablespace_name, status FROM dba_tablespaces WHERE contents = 'UNDO';` 2) `SHOW PARAMETER undo_` -- confirm undo_management=AUTO and undo_tablespace names an ONLINE tablespace. 3) Point the instance at a valid undo tablespace: `ALTER SYSTEM SET undo_tablespace = '<undo_ts>';` 4) If none exists, create one: `CREATE UNDO TABLESPACE undotbs2 DATAFILE '<path>' SIZE 8G AUTOEXTEND ON NEXT 512M MAXSIZE 32G;` then set it as above. 5) On RAC each instance needs its own undo tablespace -- check the SPFILE for per-instance settings.
ora-1555: 1) Size undo against the longest query actually run: `SELECT MAX(maxquerylen) longest_sec, MAX(tuned_undoretention) tuned_sec FROM v$undostat WHERE begin_time > SYSDATE - 7;` 2) If undo_retention is below that, raise it and make sure the tablespace can back it: `ALTER SYSTEM SET undo_retention = <seconds> SCOPE=BOTH;` then extend the undo tablespace (see ORA-30036). 3) With a fixed-size undo tablespace, Oracle auto-tunes retention downward under pressure -- an autoextensible undo tablespace is what makes undo_retention actually hold. 4) When correctness matters more than DML availability: `ALTER TABLESPACE <undo_ts> RETENTION GUARANTEE;` -- be aware this makes DML fail with ORA-30036 rather than overwrite unexpired undo. 5) For ORA-01555 on a LOB column the undo lives in the LOB segment, not the undo tablespace: `ALTER TABLE <o>.<t> MODIFY LOB (<col>) (RETENTION);` or raise PCTVERSION for BasicFile LOBs. 6) Fix the access pattern where possible: avoid fetch-across-commit (committing inside a loop that is still fetching from an open cursor), and shorten long-running reports or run them against a standby.
ora-1578: 1) Record the scope immediately: `SELECT * FROM v$database_block_corruption;` 2) Identify what the block belongs to: `SELECT owner, segment_name, segment_type, partition_name FROM dba_extents WHERE file_id = <f> AND <b> BETWEEN block_id AND block_id + blocks - 1;` 3) Find the full extent of the damage before repairing any one block: `RMAN> BACKUP VALIDATE CHECK LOGICAL DATABASE;` then re-query v$database_block_corruption. 4) Repair from backup: `RMAN> RECOVER CORRUPTION LIST;` or for a specific block `RMAN> RECOVER DATAFILE <f> BLOCK <b>;` 5) If the segment is an index and no backup exists, drop and rebuild it -- no data is lost. 6) For a table with no backup, DBMS_REPAIR can mark the block corrupt so scans skip it, at the cost of the rows it holds: `EXEC DBMS_REPAIR.FIX_CORRUPT_BLOCKS(...);` then `DBMS_REPAIR.SKIP_CORRUPT_BLOCKS`. Extract what you can first. 7) Treat the storage stack as suspect. A single ORA-01578 is frequently the first sign of failing hardware -- check the array, multipath and OS logs, and enable `db_block_checking` and `db_block_checksum` if they are off.
ora-1650: 1) This is a manual-rollback-segment error. Confirm undo mode first: `SHOW PARAMETER undo_management` -- under AUTO you should be seeing ORA-30036 instead, so check whether the instance started with a stale pfile. 2) Add space to the rollback segment tablespace: `ALTER TABLESPACE <ts> ADD DATAFILE '<path>' SIZE 2G AUTOEXTEND ON NEXT 100M MAXSIZE 16G;` 3) Migrate to Automatic Undo Management: create an undo tablespace, then `ALTER SYSTEM SET undo_management=AUTO SCOPE=SPFILE;` and `ALTER SYSTEM SET undo_tablespace='<undo_ts>' SCOPE=SPFILE;` followed by a restart.
ora-1652: 1) Identify which sessions are holding temp: `SELECT s.sid, s.serial#, s.username, s.sql_id, u.tablespace, u.blocks * t.block_size/1024/1024 mb FROM v$sort_usage u JOIN v$session s ON s.saddr = u.session_addr JOIN dba_tablespaces t ON t.tablespace_name = u.tablespace ORDER BY mb DESC;` 2) Check what is actually free: `SELECT tablespace_name, tablespace_size/1024/1024 mb, free_space/1024/1024 free_mb FROM dba_temp_free_space;` 3) Add space: `ALTER TABLESPACE TEMP ADD TEMPFILE '<path>' SIZE 4G AUTOEXTEND ON NEXT 256M MAXSIZE 32G;` 4) Space is usually the symptom, not the cause -- find the SQL: `SELECT sql_id, operation_type, max_tempseg_size/1024/1024 mb FROM v$sql_workarea_active ORDER BY max_tempseg_size DESC;` A single query spilling tens of GB normally means a bad cardinality estimate driving a huge hash join or sort. 5) Check stats on the driving tables and look for an unexpected Cartesian or a missing join predicate in the plan: `SELECT * FROM TABLE(DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_CURSOR('<sql_id>', NULL, 'ALLSTATS LAST'));` 6) If the tablespace named is permanent rather than temporary, the failing operation is a sort segment in a permanent tablespace -- treat it as ORA-01653.
ora-1653: 1) Check free space in the named tablespace: `SELECT tablespace_name, ROUND(SUM(bytes)/1024/1024) free_mb FROM dba_free_space WHERE tablespace_name = '<ts>' GROUP BY tablespace_name;` 2) Check whether autoextend still has headroom: `SELECT file_name, bytes/1024/1024 mb, maxbytes/1024/1024 max_mb, autoextensible FROM dba_data_files WHERE tablespace_name = '<ts>';` 3) Confirm the filesystem or diskgroup can back the growth before extending: `SELECT name, total_mb, free_mb FROM v$asm_diskgroup;` or `df -h` on the mount point. 4) Extend an existing file: `ALTER DATABASE DATAFILE '<file>' RESIZE <n>G;` or `ALTER DATABASE DATAFILE '<file>' AUTOEXTEND ON NEXT 512M MAXSIZE 32G;` 5) Or add a file: `ALTER TABLESPACE <ts> ADD DATAFILE '<path>' SIZE 8G AUTOEXTEND ON NEXT 512M MAXSIZE 32G;` 6) A smallfile datafile caps at roughly 32 GB with an 8 KB block size -- at that ceiling add another datafile rather than resizing, or use a bigfile tablespace.
ora-1654: 1) Handle the tablespace exactly as for ORA-01653: check dba_free_space, then dba_data_files for autoextend headroom, then extend or add a datafile. 2) Before adding space, check whether the index can simply be compacted: `SELECT index_name, tablespace_name FROM dba_indexes WHERE owner = UPPER('<o>') AND index_name = UPPER('<i>');` then `ALTER INDEX <o>.<i> REBUILD ONLINE;` 3) A rebuild needs room for both the old and new segment at once -- size the tablespace for roughly twice the index while it runs. 4) If this happens during a bulk load, consider making the index UNUSABLE for the load and rebuilding after.
ora-1688:
1) The failing partition may live in a different tablespace than the table: `SELECT partition_name, tablespace_name FROM dba_tab_partitions WHERE table_owner = UPPER('') AND table_name = UPPER('');` 2) Then extend that tablespace as for ORA-01653. 3) Check the default attributes used by new partitions: `SELECT def_tablespace_name FROM dba_part_tables WHERE owner = UPPER('') AND table_name = UPPER('');` -- with INTERVAL partitioning, every new partition lands there, so a full tablespace stops ingestion for all of them. 4) For a partition that is done being written, consider compressing it: `ALTER TABLE . MOVE PARTITION

COMPRESS;`
ora-1691: 1) Find the LOB segment and its tablespace: `SELECT column_name, segment_name, tablespace_name FROM dba_lobs WHERE owner = UPPER('<o>') AND table_name = UPPER('<t>');` 2) Extend that tablespace as for ORA-01653. 3) For SecureFile LOBs, undo retention holds old versions inside the segment -- check the retention setting: `SELECT column_name, retention_type, retention_value FROM dba_lobs WHERE owner = UPPER('<o>') AND table_name = UPPER('<t>');` 4) For BasicFile LOBs, PCTVERSION or RETENTION can pin large amounts of space; frequent LOB update workloads grow far beyond the visible data size. 5) Reclaim after deletes: `ALTER TABLE <o>.<t> MODIFY LOB (<col>) (SHRINK SPACE);`
ora-1950: 1) Same root cause as ORA-01536: the user has no quota on the target tablespace. `SELECT tablespace_name, max_bytes FROM dba_ts_quotas WHERE username = UPPER('<user>');` 2) Grant quota: `ALTER USER <user> QUOTA UNLIMITED ON <ts>;` 3) Note that UNLIMITED TABLESPACE as a system privilege overrides individual quotas and is usually too broad -- prefer an explicit per-tablespace quota. 4) Check the user's default tablespace if the statement did not name one: `SELECT username, default_tablespace, temporary_tablespace FROM dba_users WHERE username = UPPER('<user>');`
ora-2292: 1) Identify the constraint and both tables: `SELECT owner, constraint_name, table_name, r_owner, r_constraint_name FROM dba_constraints WHERE constraint_name = UPPER('<c>');` then look up the referenced constraint to get the parent table. 2) Find the blocking children: `SELECT * FROM <child_table> WHERE <fk_col> = <parent_key_value>;` 3) Delete or reparent the children first, or redefine the constraint if cascading matches the data model: `ALTER TABLE <child> DROP CONSTRAINT <c>; ALTER TABLE <child> ADD CONSTRAINT <c> FOREIGN KEY (<col>) REFERENCES <parent>(<col>) ON DELETE CASCADE;` 4) ON DELETE CASCADE is a data-model decision, not a workaround -- confirm the children should really disappear with the parent. 5) While here, verify the child FK columns are indexed. An unindexed foreign key makes every parent delete take a full table lock on the child and is a leading cause of ORA-00054 and ORA-00060: `SELECT index_name, column_name, column_position FROM dba_ind_columns WHERE table_name = UPPER('<child>');`
ora-2391: 1) A profile limit, not an instance limit. `SELECT p.profile, p.resource_name, p.limit FROM dba_profiles p WHERE p.resource_name = 'SESSIONS_PER_USER';` 2) Which profile the user has: `SELECT username, profile FROM dba_users WHERE username = UPPER('<u>');` 3) Current count: `SELECT username, COUNT(*) FROM v$session WHERE username = UPPER('<u>') GROUP BY username;` 4) Raise it: `ALTER PROFILE <profile> LIMIT SESSIONS_PER_USER <n>;` (takes effect immediately, no restart). 5) Confirm resource_limit is enforced at all: `SHOW PARAMETER resource_limit` -- it is TRUE by default in 12c+. 6) If a connection pool is the client, cap the pool below the profile limit rather than raising the limit.
ora-3113: 1) This is a symptom: the server process went away. It is never the root cause, so do not tune the network until the alert log is ruled out. `SELECT value FROM v$diag_info WHERE name IN ('Diag Trace','Diag Alert');` 2) Look in the alert log at the exact timestamp for ORA-00600, ORA-07445, a process termination, or an instance crash. 3) Check the OS for the process being killed externally -- the Linux OOM killer in `dmesg` or /var/log/messages is a common cause under memory pressure. 4) If it happens only on idle connections after a fixed interval, it is a firewall or load-balancer idle timeout. Set `SQLNET.EXPIRE_TIME = 10` in the server sqlnet.ora and enable TCP keepalive. 5) If it reproduces with one specific statement, it is a server-side crash on that plan -- capture the incident (`adrci> show incident`) and open an SR. 6) Check for a killed session: `SELECT sid, serial#, status FROM v$session WHERE status = 'KILLED';` and review whether a resource manager plan or a DBA script is terminating sessions.
ora-3136: 1) Authentication did not complete inside the timeout. Check both settings: SQLNET.INBOUND_CONNECT_TIMEOUT in the server sqlnet.ora (default 60s) and INBOUND_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_<listener> in listener.ora. 2) Check the listener log for the source host -- repeated entries from one address are often a port scanner or a health check that opens a socket and never authenticates. 3) If authentication is genuinely slow (LDAP, Kerberos, a loaded host), raise both values rather than disabling them; setting either to 0 removes protection against connection-exhaustion attacks. 4) Check host load and whether the listener is starved: a CPU-saturated host produces this under load. 5) Correlate with ORA-00020 -- an instance at its process limit makes authentication hang long enough to hit the timeout.
ora-3297: 1) The resize floor is the highest allocated block in the file, not the amount of data: `SELECT file_id, MAX(block_id + blocks - 1) hwm_blocks FROM dba_extents WHERE file_id = <n> GROUP BY file_id;` 2) Convert to a size: multiply hwm_blocks by the block size, then resize to slightly above that. 3) To shrink further, move the segments sitting above the high water mark: `SELECT owner, segment_name, segment_type FROM dba_extents WHERE file_id = <n> AND block_id > <hwm> GROUP BY owner, segment_name, segment_type;` then `ALTER TABLE <o>.<t> MOVE;` or `ALTER INDEX <o>.<i> REBUILD;` and retry the resize. 4) Remember that MOVE invalidates indexes on the table: `ALTER TABLE <o>.<t> MOVE ONLINE;` maintains them, otherwise rebuild afterwards.
ora-4020: 1) This is a library cache (DDL) deadlock, not a row-level one. Find what holds the object: `SELECT s.sid, s.serial#, s.username, s.program, d.name, d.type, d.mode_held, d.mode_requested FROM dba_ddl_locks d JOIN v$session s ON s.sid = d.session_id WHERE d.name = UPPER('<object>');` 2) The usual trigger is a package being recompiled while sessions are executing it, or two sessions compiling interdependent objects at once. 3) Terminate the holder if the compile must proceed: `ALTER SYSTEM KILL SESSION '<sid>,<serial#>' IMMEDIATE;` 4) Serialize deployments: recompile in a maintenance window, or use `utlrp.sql` when the application is quiesced. 5) Edition-Based Redefinition avoids this class of error entirely for online code changes.
ora-4021: 1) Same cause as ORA-04020 but surfaced as a timeout. Identify the holder with dba_ddl_locks as above. 2) `SELECT sid, event, seconds_in_wait, p1, p2 FROM v$session WHERE event LIKE 'library cache%';` 3) Kill the blocking session or retry once it finishes. 4) If a long-running job holds the object for hours, the fix is scheduling, not a longer timeout.
ora-4030: 1) This is process-private memory (PGA), not the SGA. Check the instance total: `SELECT name, value/1024/1024 mb FROM v$pgastat WHERE name IN ('total PGA allocated','total PGA inuse','aggregate PGA target parameter','over allocation count');` 2) Find the consuming process: `SELECT s.sid, s.username, s.program, p.pga_used_mem/1024/1024 used_mb, p.pga_max_mem/1024/1024 max_mb FROM v$process p JOIN v$session s ON s.paddr = p.addr ORDER BY p.pga_max_mem DESC FETCH FIRST 20 ROWS ONLY;` 3) Check the OS before the database: free RAM, swap, and the per-process address-space limit (`ulimit -v`, `ulimit -s`) for the oracle user. On Linux also check vm.max_map_count and any cgroup memory limit. 4) The usual application cause is an unbounded BULK COLLECT or a PL/SQL collection built in memory -- add a `LIMIT` clause and process in batches. 5) Raise pga_aggregate_target only if the host genuinely has the memory: `ALTER SYSTEM SET pga_aggregate_target = <n>G SCOPE=BOTH;` 6) Note that pga_aggregate_target is a target, not a cap -- PGA can exceed it, which is why the host runs out before the parameter does.
ora-4031: 1) This is shared memory (SGA). See where it went: `SELECT pool, name, bytes/1024/1024 mb FROM v$sgastat WHERE pool = 'shared pool' ORDER BY bytes DESC FETCH FIRST 20 ROWS ONLY;` 2) The dominant cause is literal SQL flooding the library cache. Confirm it: `SELECT force_matching_signature, COUNT(*) versions, MIN(sql_text) sample FROM v$sql WHERE force_matching_signature <> 0 GROUP BY force_matching_signature HAVING COUNT(*) > 50 ORDER BY versions DESC;` Hundreds of near-identical statements means the application is not using bind variables. 3) The correct fix is bind variables in the application. `ALTER SYSTEM SET cursor_sharing = FORCE;` is a stopgap that has its own plan-stability costs. 4) Also check for high version counts on a single statement: `SELECT sql_id, version_count FROM v$sqlarea WHERE version_count > 50 ORDER BY version_count DESC;` then `SELECT * FROM v$sql_shared_cursor WHERE sql_id = '<id>';` to see why cursors are not being shared. 5) Size the pool: `SELECT shared_pool_size_for_estimate mb, estd_lc_time_saved FROM v$shared_pool_advice;` then raise sga_target or shared_pool_size if the advisory shows benefit. 6) `ALTER SYSTEM FLUSH SHARED_POOL;` is emergency relief only -- expect a hard-parse storm immediately after, and it does nothing about the cause.
ora-4036: 1) The instance or PDB crossed pga_aggregate_limit and Oracle is terminating the largest PGA consumers to enforce it. `SHOW PARAMETER pga_aggregate` 2) Identify the consumers before raising anything: `SELECT s.sid, s.username, s.program, p.pga_used_mem/1024/1024 used_mb FROM v$process p JOIN v$session s ON s.paddr = p.addr ORDER BY p.pga_used_mem DESC FETCH FIRST 20 ROWS ONLY;` 3) `SELECT name, value/1024/1024 mb FROM v$pgastat WHERE name LIKE '%PGA%';` 4) Raise the limit only with RAM to back it: `ALTER SYSTEM SET pga_aggregate_limit = <n>G SCOPE=BOTH;` Setting it to 0 disables the protection and lets the host run out of memory instead -- do not. 5) In a CDB, the limit can be set per PDB; check whether one PDB is starving the rest. 6) Treat the underlying runaway SQL or PL/SQL as for ORA-04030.
ora-4061: 1) A dependency changed and this object's compiled state is stale. Usually the next call succeeds after automatic recompilation -- the application should retry once. 2) If it does not recover, the object has real errors: `SELECT line, text FROM dba_errors WHERE owner = UPPER('<o>') AND name = UPPER('<n>') ORDER BY sequence;` -- then treat as ORA-04063. 3) Find the trigger for the invalidation: `SELECT object_name, object_type, last_ddl_time FROM dba_objects WHERE last_ddl_time > SYSDATE - 1 ORDER BY last_ddl_time DESC;` 4) Recompile the dependency tree: `EXEC UTL_RECOMP.RECOMP_PARALLEL(4);` 5) Repeated occurrences in business hours mean DDL is being applied live -- move schema changes to a window, or adopt Edition-Based Redefinition.
ora-4063:
1) The object compiled with errors. Read them: `SELECT line, position, text FROM dba_errors WHERE owner = UPPER('') AND name = UPPER('') ORDER BY sequence;` 2) List everything invalid: `SELECT owner, object_name, object_type FROM dba_objects WHERE status = 'INVALID' ORDER BY owner, object_name;` 3) Recompiling will not fix a genuine error, but it will clear objects invalidated only by a dependency change: `ALTER PACKAGE .

COMPILE; ALTER PACKAGE .

COMPILE BODY;` or in bulk `@?/rdbms/admin/utlrp.sql` / `EXEC UTL_RECOMP.RECOMP_PARALLEL(4);` 4) If the errors are 'table or view does not exist' style, the owner is missing a grant -- see ORA-00942, and grant directly rather than through a role. 5) Find what invalidated it: `SELECT owner, name, type, referenced_owner, referenced_name FROM dba_dependencies WHERE referenced_name = UPPER('');`
ora-4068: 1) Harmless in isolation: a package with global state was recompiled while this session held instantiated state, so the state was discarded. The session's next call succeeds -- the application should catch and retry once. 2) Find what was recompiled: `SELECT owner, object_name, object_type, last_ddl_time FROM dba_objects WHERE object_type LIKE 'PACKAGE%' AND last_ddl_time > SYSDATE - 1 ORDER BY last_ddl_time DESC;` 3) If it happens constantly, something is invalidating packages continuously -- look for a job recompiling objects or DDL on a dependency: `SELECT * FROM dba_dependencies WHERE referenced_name = UPPER('<obj>');` 4) Stop recompiling packages with package-level variables during business hours. 5) `PRAGMA SERIALLY_REUSABLE` or Edition-Based Redefinition removes the exposure for code that must change online.
ora-6502: 1) The accompanying ORA-06512 gives the line number. Map it to source: `SELECT line, text FROM dba_source WHERE owner = UPPER('<o>') AND name = UPPER('<n>') AND type = '<TYPE>' AND line BETWEEN <l> - 5 AND <l> + 5 ORDER BY line;` 2) The usual causes are: a string assigned to a VARCHAR2 variable declared too short, a non-numeric string assigned to NUMBER, a value exceeding a NUMBER's precision, or NULL assigned to a NOT NULL variable. 3) Declare variables with %TYPE so they track the column and cannot drift: `v_name <table>.<col>%TYPE;` 4) A common trap is a local VARCHAR2(n) receiving a column that was later widened -- compare the two: `SELECT data_length, char_length FROM dba_tab_columns WHERE table_name = UPPER('<t>') AND column_name = UPPER('<c>');` 5) Add DBMS_UTILITY.FORMAT_ERROR_BACKTRACE to the exception handler so the failing line is reported in production rather than inferred.
ora-6550:
1) ORA-06550 is a wrapper -- the embedded PLS- message is the real error. Read the full text, including the line and column it gives. 2) If it refers to a stored object, get its errors: `SELECT line, position, text FROM dba_errors WHERE owner = UPPER('') AND name = UPPER('') ORDER BY sequence;` 3) PLS-00306 (wrong number or types of arguments) is most often a signature change the caller has not picked up, or a NULL passed where the overload cannot be resolved: `SELECT argument_name, position, data_type, in_out FROM dba_arguments WHERE owner = UPPER('') AND object_name = UPPER('

') ORDER BY position;` 4) PLS-00201 (identifier must be declared) usually means the caller cannot see the object at all -- treat it as ORA-00942, and remember roles do not apply inside definer-rights PL/SQL. 5) For dynamic SQL built at runtime, print the statement before executing it; the line and column refer to the generated text, not the source.
ora-7445: 1) A server process took an OS exception and dumped core -- handle it like ORA-00600. The arguments include the failing function, which is what identifies it. 2) `adrci> show incident` then `adrci> show trace <file>` for the call stack. 3) Look the failing function up in MOS Doc 153788.1. 4) Package for support: `adrci> ips pack incident <n> in /tmp` 5) Rule out environmental causes first: memory pressure and OOM kills (`dmesg`), a partially applied patch, a relinked binary that failed, or a corrupt $ORACLE_HOME. 6) Check whether the instance survived and whether sessions were affected: `SELECT instance_name, status, startup_time FROM v$instance;` 7) Open an SR with the packaged incident.
ora-8103: 1) Either a concurrent DDL removed the segment under an open cursor, or the segment header is inconsistent. Establish which. 2) Check for recent DDL on the object: `SELECT owner, object_name, object_type, last_ddl_time FROM dba_objects WHERE object_name = UPPER('<obj>');` A TRUNCATE or MOVE concurrent with a long query produces this legitimately -- serialize them. 3) If no DDL is involved, test the structure: `ANALYZE TABLE <o>.<t> VALIDATE STRUCTURE CASCADE;` 4) `RMAN> VALIDATE DATAFILE <f>;` for the segment's files, then `SELECT * FROM v$database_block_corruption;` 5) For a partitioned table, check whether a partition was dropped or exchanged during the query. 6) If structural damage is confirmed, treat it as ORA-01578 and recover from backup.
ora-12154: 1) Purely client-side name resolution -- the database was never contacted. Find which tnsnames.ora is actually in use: `echo $TNS_ADMIN` and check $ORACLE_HOME/network/admin as the fallback. 2) `tnsping <alias>` -- it prints the file it read and the descriptor it resolved. 3) A syntax error such as an unbalanced parenthesis silently breaks every entry after it in the file, so a recently added alias can break unrelated ones. 4) Check sqlnet.ora NAMES.DIRECTORY_PATH -- if it lists only LDAP or ONAMES, tnsnames.ora is not consulted. 5) For EZConnect, the form is `host:port/service_name`; a SID will not work there. 6) Confirm the service name on the server: `SELECT name FROM v$services;` 7) On Windows or in an IDE, a stale TNS_ADMIN in the environment or registry is a frequent cause.
ora-12514: 1) The listener answered but does not know that service. `lsnrctl services` on the database host -- look for the service and its handler state. 2) On the instance: `SELECT name FROM v$services;` and `SHOW PARAMETER service_names` 3) Force a registration rather than waiting for the next PMON cycle: `ALTER SYSTEM REGISTER;` 4) If the instance is down, mounting, or still opening, its services are not registered -- check `SELECT status FROM v$instance;` and the alert log. 5) With a non-default listener port or a remote listener, local_listener must point at it: `SHOW PARAMETER local_listener` and `SHOW PARAMETER remote_listener` 6) Connecting by SID instead of SERVICE_NAME needs a SID_LIST_<listener> entry in listener.ora; prefer SERVICE_NAME. 7) In a CDB, a PDB's service only exists while the PDB is open: `SELECT name, open_mode FROM v$pdbs;`
ora-12516: 1) The listener found the service but no handler would take the connection -- this is usually the instance at its process or session ceiling. `SELECT resource_name, current_utilization, max_utilization, limit_value FROM v$resource_limit WHERE resource_name IN ('processes','sessions');` 2) `lsnrctl services` shows the dispatcher or dedicated handler state; 'blocked' confirms the instance is refusing new connections. 3) Treat it as ORA-00020 -- raise processes and restart, or reduce the client pool. 4) With shared servers, check dispatcher capacity too: `SELECT name, status, accept, busy, idle FROM v$dispatcher;` and `SHOW PARAMETER dispatchers` 5) A connection storm at startup (every pool member connecting at once) can trip this transiently -- stagger pool warm-up.
ora-12541: 1) No listener is answering at that host and port. On the database host: `lsnrctl status` 2) Confirm the port matches the connect descriptor and that the listener is bound to the address the client is using -- `lsnrctl status` prints the listening endpoints. 3) Check the network path independently: `telnet <host> <port>` or `nc -vz <host> <port>`. A firewall drop usually looks like a timeout; an outright refusal looks like this. 4) Start it: `lsnrctl start <listener_name>` 5) On RAC or Grid Infrastructure use srvctl, not lsnrctl: `srvctl status listener` and `srvctl status scan_listener`; start with `srvctl start listener`. 6) If the listener runs but on a different ORACLE_HOME than expected, check which one by its process and the listener.ora that home uses.
ora-12801: 1) ORA-12801 is a wrapper. The error immediately following it is the real failure -- diagnose that one (commonly ORA-01652 for temp, ORA-04030 for PGA). 2) Check parallel capacity: `SELECT resource_name, current_utilization, max_utilization, limit_value FROM v$resource_limit WHERE resource_name IN ('parallel_max_servers','processes');` 3) `SELECT * FROM v$px_process WHERE status <> 'AVAILABLE';` and `SELECT name, value FROM v$sysstat WHERE name LIKE 'Parallel operations%';` -- a high 'downgraded' count means slaves are unavailable. 4) Confirm whether parallelism is the trigger by reproducing serially: `ALTER SESSION DISABLE PARALLEL QUERY;` If it then succeeds, the problem is per-slave resource limits, not the query logic. 5) Each slave consumes its own PGA and temp allocation, so a degree of 32 multiplies the footprint 32 times -- cap it: `ALTER TABLE <t> PARALLEL (DEGREE 8);` or use a hint. 6) Check that parallel_max_servers and processes are sized together; exhausting slaves surfaces here.
ora-12899: 1) The message gives the column, the actual length and the maximum -- start from those numbers. 2) Check whether the column uses byte or character semantics: `SELECT column_name, data_type, data_length, char_length, char_used FROM dba_tab_columns WHERE owner = UPPER('<o>') AND table_name = UPPER('<t>');` char_used of 'B' means a VARCHAR2(10) holds 10 bytes, which is fewer than 10 characters in a multibyte character set. 3) This is the single most common failure after a migration to AL32UTF8. If actual is at most 4x maximum and the data looks correct, the column is sized in bytes, not the data too large: `ALTER TABLE <o>.<t> MODIFY (<col> VARCHAR2(<n> CHAR));` 4) Otherwise widen it: `ALTER TABLE <o>.<t> MODIFY (<col> VARCHAR2(<n>));` 5) To make new columns default to character semantics: `ALTER SESSION SET nls_length_semantics = CHAR;` (and consider the instance parameter for new schemas). 6) Find the offending source rows: `SELECT * FROM <source> WHERE LENGTHB(<col>) > <max>;` -- LENGTHB, not LENGTH, is what the error measures.
ora-15041: 1) From an ASM instance: `SELECT name, type, total_mb, free_mb, required_mirror_free_mb, usable_file_mb FROM v$asm_diskgroup;` 2) usable_file_mb is the number that matters -- it accounts for redundancy. When it goes negative the diskgroup can no longer survive a disk failure even if free_mb looks healthy. 3) Add capacity: `ALTER DISKGROUP <dg> ADD DISK '<path>' REBALANCE POWER 8;` then watch `SELECT * FROM v$asm_operation;` until the rebalance completes. 4) See what is consuming it: `asmcmd du -H +<dg>` and `asmcmd ls -ls +<dg>/<db>/ARCHIVELOG/` 5) If it is the FRA diskgroup, the cause is usually unreclaimed archivelogs -- treat it as ORA-00257 first. 6) Check for a stalled rebalance holding space: `SELECT group_number, operation, state, est_minutes FROM v$asm_operation;` 7) Removing a disk also needs free space to rebalance into -- do not drop disks to make room.
ora-15080: 1) A physical I/O to an ASM disk failed. Identify it: `SELECT group_number, disk_number, name, path, mode_status, state, header_status FROM v$asm_disk WHERE mode_status <> 'ONLINE' OR state <> 'NORMAL';` 2) Check the OS layer -- `dmesg` and /var/log/messages for SCSI or multipath errors, and `multipath -ll` for a failed path. Confirm: `SELECT * FROM v$asm_operation;` 4) Verify the diskgroup can still tolerate the loss: `SELECT name, type, usable_file_mb FROM v$asm_diskgroup;` -- see ORA-15041 if usable space is negative. 5) With EXTERNAL redundancy there is no ASM-level protection, so a disk failure is a restore situation -- check for corruption: `SELECT * FROM v$database_block_corruption;` 6) After the hardware is replaced: `ALTER DISKGROUP <dg> ONLINE DISK <name>;` or add the replacement and let it rebalance.
ora-16038: 1) The log cannot be archived, so redo will stall once it wraps. Check the destinations: `SELECT dest_id, status, error, destination FROM v$archive_dest WHERE status = 'ERROR';` 2) Most often the FRA is full -- follow ORA-00257. 3) Check the log group's state: `SELECT group#, sequence#, archived, status FROM v$log;` and `SELECT * FROM v$archive_dest_status WHERE status <> 'VALID';` 4) After clearing the underlying problem: `ALTER SYSTEM ARCHIVE LOG ALL;` 5) If a member is corrupt and the log is already archived elsewhere, `ALTER DATABASE CLEAR LOGFILE GROUP <n>;` -- use `CLEAR UNARCHIVED LOGFILE` only as a last resort, as it breaks recoverability and requires a fresh backup.
ora-19809: 1) Same condition as ORA-00257 -- the recovery area has hit db_recovery_file_dest_size. `SELECT * FROM v$recovery_file_dest;` 2) `SELECT file_type, percent_space_used, percent_space_reclaimable FROM v$flash_recovery_area_usage;` -- a high reclaimable percentage means a backup will free it; a low one means the limit is genuinely too small. 3) Back up and delete archivelogs, or raise db_recovery_file_dest_size. See ORA-00257 for the full sequence. 4) Check for orphaned flashback logs and obsolete backups: `RMAN> DELETE OBSOLETE;` and review the retention policy with `RMAN> SHOW RETENTION POLICY;`
ora-19815: 1) This is a warning, not yet an outage -- act before it becomes ORA-00257. `SELECT name, space_limit/1024/1024/1024 limit_gb, space_used/1024/1024/1024 used_gb FROM v$recovery_file_dest;` 2) `SELECT file_type, percent_space_used, percent_space_reclaimable FROM v$flash_recovery_area_usage;` 3) Run the archivelog backup ahead of schedule, or raise db_recovery_file_dest_size. 4) If this recurs on a cycle, the FRA is sized below one backup interval's worth of redo -- size it from peak redo rate: `SELECT TRUNC(completion_time) day, SUM(blocks*block_size)/1024/1024/1024 gb FROM v$archived_log GROUP BY TRUNC(completion_time) ORDER BY 1 DESC FETCH FIRST 14 ROWS ONLY;`
ora-27037: 1) An OS-level failure. The 'Additional information' and OS error number in the full stack identify the actual cause -- read them before anything else. 2) Verify the file exists and the oracle OS user can read it: `ls -l <path>` as the oracle user, not as root. 3) For ASM, confirm the diskgroup is mounted and the disks are online: `SELECT name, state, type FROM v$asm_diskgroup;` and `SELECT path, mode_status, header_status FROM v$asm_disk WHERE mode_status <> 'ONLINE';` 4) Common causes: an NFS mount that dropped (check `mount` and the NFS options -- Oracle requires specific ones), a file removed outside the database, wrong ownership after a restore, or a symlink to a path that no longer exists. 5) Cross-check what the database expects: `SELECT name FROM v$datafile UNION ALL SELECT name FROM v$controlfile UNION ALL SELECT member FROM v$logfile;` and confirm each path resolves. 6) If the file is genuinely gone, restore it: `RMAN> RESTORE DATAFILE <f>; RECOVER DATAFILE <f>;`
ora-28000: 1) Confirm and see when it locked: `SELECT username, account_status, lock_date, profile FROM dba_users WHERE username = UPPER('<user>');` 2) Find what locked it before unlocking, or it will relock within minutes: `SELECT dbusername, userhost, client_program_name, COUNT(*), MAX(event_timestamp) FROM unified_audit_trail WHERE return_code = 1017 AND dbusername = UPPER('<user>') GROUP BY dbusername, userhost, client_program_name ORDER BY 4 DESC;` The offending host and program are almost always a service with an outdated password. 3) Check the threshold: `SELECT limit FROM dba_profiles WHERE profile = (SELECT profile FROM dba_users WHERE username = UPPER('<user>')) AND resource_name = 'FAILED_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS';` 4) Unlock: `ALTER USER <user> ACCOUNT UNLOCK;` 5) account_status of EXPIRED(GRACE) & LOCKED(TIMED) needs both an unlock and a password reset. 6) For service accounts that must never lock, move them to a profile with FAILED_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS UNLIMITED -- but only alongside a network-level control, since that removes brute-force protection.
ora-28001: 1) `SELECT username, account_status, expiry_date, profile FROM dba_users WHERE username = UPPER('<user>');` 2) Reset the password: `ALTER USER <user> IDENTIFIED BY "<new_password>";` 3) To reset without knowing or changing the password, reapply the existing hash: `SELECT name, spare4 FROM sys.user$ WHERE name = UPPER('<user>');` then `ALTER USER <user> IDENTIFIED BY VALUES '<spare4>';` -- this clears the expiry while keeping the credential. 4) Stop it recurring for service accounts: `ALTER PROFILE <profile> LIMIT PASSWORD_LIFE_TIME UNLIMITED;` or move the account to a dedicated profile. 5) The DEFAULT profile has PASSWORD_LIFE_TIME 180 since 11g, so this arrives on a schedule after any upgrade or new build -- audit for it: `SELECT username, expiry_date FROM dba_users WHERE expiry_date < SYSDATE + 30 AND account_status <> 'OPEN' ORDER BY expiry_date;`
ora-28002: 1) A grace-period warning, not yet a failure -- fix it before it becomes ORA-28001. `SELECT username, account_status, expiry_date, profile FROM dba_users WHERE expiry_date < SYSDATE + 14 ORDER BY expiry_date;` 2) Reset the password, or reapply the existing hash to reset the clock (see ORA-28001 step 3). 3) For service accounts: `ALTER PROFILE <profile> LIMIT PASSWORD_LIFE_TIME UNLIMITED;` 4) Some connection pools treat the warning as a fatal error and refuse to connect -- do not wait for the grace period to run out.
ora-29740: 1) A RAC instance was evicted. Reconstruct the timeline from all nodes: the alert log on each instance plus $ORACLE_BASE/diag/crs/<node>/crs/trace/ocssd.trc and the LMON trace named in the alert log. 2) The three usual causes are interconnect packet loss, a node hung under CPU or memory starvation, and storage or voting-disk I/O stalls. Determine which before changing any timeout. 3) `oclumon dumpnodeview -allnodes -last "00:30:00"` for CPU, memory and network at the eviction moment. 4) Verify the interconnect: `oifcfg getif`, then check the private NIC for drops and errors (`ip -s link`, `netstat -s`). Confirm the database is actually using it: `SELECT name, ip_address FROM v$cluster_interconnects;` 5) Check for chronic interconnect pressure in AWR -- 'gc cr block lost' and 'gc current block lost' are nonzero only when the network is dropping traffic: `SELECT name, value FROM v$sysstat WHERE name LIKE 'gc%lost%';` 6) Check voting disk and storage latency; an I/O stall longer than the CSS misscount evicts the node. 7) Raising misscount is not a fix and masks the real fault -- change it only on Oracle Support's instruction.
ora-30032: 1) Find the suspended statement and the error that suspended it: `SELECT session_id, instance_id, status, error_number, error_msg, suspend_time, sql_text FROM dba_resumable;` 2) The error_msg column names the real problem -- almost always a space error (ORA-01653, ORA-30036, ORA-01652). Fix that first. 3) Extend the resumable window if the fix legitimately takes longer: `ALTER SESSION ENABLE RESUMABLE TIMEOUT 7200;` or `ALTER SYSTEM SET resumable_timeout = 7200 SCOPE=BOTH;` 4) Set up notification so the next one is caught before it times out -- an AFTER SUSPEND trigger or an alert on dba_resumable.
ora-30036: 1) Check free space in the active undo tablespace: `SELECT tablespace_name, ROUND(SUM(bytes)/1024/1024) free_mb FROM dba_free_space WHERE tablespace_name = (SELECT value FROM v$parameter WHERE name = 'undo_tablespace') GROUP BY tablespace_name;` 2) Look for a long-running transaction pinning undo: `SELECT s.sid, s.serial#, s.username, t.used_ublk * 8192/1024/1024 mb, t.start_time FROM v$transaction t JOIN v$session s ON s.saddr = t.ses_addr ORDER BY mb DESC;` 3) Check retention pressure: `SELECT MAX(tuned_undoretention) tuned, MAX(maxquerylen) longest_query FROM v$undostat WHERE begin_time > SYSDATE - 1;` 4) Add space: `ALTER TABLESPACE <undo_ts> ADD DATAFILE '<path>' SIZE 8G AUTOEXTEND ON NEXT 512M MAXSIZE 32G;` 5) If RETENTION GUARANTEE is set, undo cannot be reused even when expired: `SELECT tablespace_name, retention FROM dba_tablespaces WHERE contents = 'UNDO';` Turning it off with `ALTER TABLESPACE <undo_ts> RETENTION NOGUARANTEE;` clears the error but trades it for ORA-01555 risk -- add space first if the guarantee was deliberate.
ora-30926: 1) A MERGE or updatable-join UPDATE matched the same target row more than once. Find the duplicates in the source: `SELECT <join_cols>, COUNT(*) FROM (<source query>) GROUP BY <join_cols> HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;` 2) Fix the source -- de-duplicate, add the missing predicate, or pick a winner explicitly with a window function (`ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY <join_cols> ORDER BY <tiebreak>) = 1`). 3) Do not paper over it with DISTINCT: that hides which row won and makes the result non-deterministic. 4) If the source is correct and the target has duplicate keys, check for a missing unique constraint on the join columns: `SELECT constraint_name, constraint_type FROM dba_constraints WHERE table_name = UPPER('<t>');`
ora-65114: 1) The PDB has hit its storage limit. Check it: `SELECT con_id, property_name, property_value FROM cdb_properties WHERE property_name LIKE 'MAX_%STORAGE%';` or from inside the PDB `SELECT * FROM dba_pdb_history;` and the DDL in `SELECT dbms_metadata.get_ddl('PLUGGABLE DATABASE','<pdb>') FROM dual;` 2) See what the PDB is using: `SELECT tablespace_name, SUM(bytes)/1024/1024/1024 gb FROM cdb_data_files WHERE con_id = <n> GROUP BY tablespace_name ORDER BY 2 DESC;` 3) Raise the limit: `ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE <pdb> STORAGE (MAXSIZE <n>G);` or remove it with `STORAGE UNLIMITED`. 4) Confirm the CDB and the underlying filesystem or diskgroup can back the increase before raising it. 5) Alternatively reclaim inside the PDB -- drop unused segments, shrink datafiles (see ORA-03297), or move cold data out. 6) MAX_SHARED_TEMP_SIZE has its own limit; if the failure is on temp, raise that instead.
